title: Patience

segments.voice: Yesterday, hope: Paul's riddle, hope that is seen is not hope. Your line was hope unseen. Did you say not yet to something that looked finished? Day one thousand four hundred eight.

A farmer has done everything a farmer can do. The field is plowed, the seed is in, the fence is mended. Now there is nothing left but the sky. He can't make it rain. He can't pull the shoots up out of the ground to hurry them. He can only stand at the edge of the field in the evening and wait. The letter of James holds up that farmer as a picture, and yesterday Paul ended his riddle about hope with the same quiet word: we wait for it with patience. Today: patience.

Here is James, in the King James words: "Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain." Precious fruit. The farmer isn't bored. He's waiting for something he loves. That's the turn in today's lesson. In the Bible, patience isn't only putting up with things. It is a kind of love. Paul's chapter on love starts its list right here: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind." Charity is the King James word for love. And the first thing it says love does is suffer long. Love waits. Then the Bible turns the same word toward God. When God passes before Moses on the mountain, he names himself: "The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth." Longsuffering. God's patience is part of his own name in that passage. And a letter of Peter answers people asking why the Lord's promised coming seems slow, in words that are surprisingly tender: "The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish." If God seems slow, Peter says, it's because God is waiting for people. Love that waits. So patience, here, isn't a gritted jaw. It's the farmer at the fence, the parent at the door at midnight, the friend who lets you take your time. And for Christians it's also the way God waits for them. Being patient with someone, in this picture, means loving them at their speed.

Here's the practice: wait patiently for one thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you're waiting for right now. A person to change. An answer. A healing. A slow project. Notice how your body holds the waiting: a tight jaw, a restless hand. Breathe into that place and let it loosen a little. Then ask: what would it look like to wait for this the way the farmer waits, for something precious? If you pray, you can bring it to God in James's words, be patient therefore. Then let the bell hold you, without hurrying it. The bell holds the time.
Patience. In the Bible, longsuffering: the farmer's wait for precious fruit, the first thing love does, and the way God himself waits.
Your line: love waits. Today, when someone is slow, late, or not ready, try waiting for them the way you'd wait for something precious, with no sigh at the end. Day one thousand four hundred eight.

howItsDone: Christians count patience, called longsuffering in the King James Bible, among the fruit of the Spirit; churches teach it as something grown over a lifetime of prayer and practice.

fork.setup: you're the farmer in James. the seed is in, and the rain hasn't come. what do you do?
options: pull up the shoots to see if they're growing.
wait with long patience for the early and latter rain.
fork.reveal: the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it. he waits because the fruit is precious to him.

original.note: Greek: patience, longsuffering — the word family behind "suffereth long" in 1 Corinthians 13:4.

trapdoor: what you thought: patience means gritting your teeth until it's over.
what it means: in the Bible, patience is love that waits, and God waits too.
what a scholar hears: makrothumia: one Greek word family names the patience of love in 1 Corinthians 13 and the long patience of the farmer in James 5.
recall: Catholic and Orthodox word for it
